short: A physician with a master’s in biological sciences who grew up with black seed in the kitchen cupboard and got tired of guessing what was in the bottle.
lede: Say exactly what is inside. Test every lot. Publish the results.
why: Black seed was in my house before I knew what a molecule was. My mother kept it next to the salt. In my master’s work and then in medical school I kept running into the same gap: a seed with centuries of use across Unani, Ayurvedic, and Chinese practice, and almost no honest labeling. Bottles sold on a saying with no lot number. Oils refined until they were pale and tasteless. No certificate anywhere.

This company is my answer to that gap. We buy one harvest from one documented supplier. We press it cold. We send every lot to an independent laboratory, and we publish what the laboratory found, in the laboratory’s own words.
If a bottle does not match its certificate, or you simply do not love it, I would rather refund you than have you keep it. That is the whole standard.

title: A seed with a long story.
paragraphs: Nigella sativa is a small annual in the buttercup family, grown for its black, angular seeds across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. Seeds were found in Tutankhamun’s tomb, and the plant appears in the Old Testament under the name ketzah, where the prophet Isaiah describes it being threshed with a stick rather than a sledge.

In the kitchen it is kalonji, habbat al-barakah, çörek otu, or siyah daneh depending on where you are standing. It is pressed into naan and sprinkled over simit, tempered in hot oil for dal, folded into Bengali panch phoron, and stirred into string cheese in the Levant. The oil was pressed for the table long before it was bottled for anything else.

In Islamic tradition the seed holds a place of its own. The narration quoted below is why a jar of it sits in so many homes, passed from one generation to the next with the salt and the honey. We keep that tradition by getting the seed itself right. The seed is a food and a story; we make no claim beyond that.

hadith.narration: “There is healing in black seed for all diseases except death.”
hadith.attribution: Narrated by Abu Hurairah, Sahih al-Bukhari 5688, Book 76 (Medicine)
hadith.note: We quote this narration because it is why black seed has been kept in homes across the Muslim world for fourteen centuries. We quote it for heritage, not as evidence. It is not a product claim and not medical advice, and we have not evaluated it as either.

title: Every lot, tested. Every number, published.
body: Each pressing gets an independent lab panel covering thymoquinone, fatty-acid profile, freshness, heavy metals, and microbial screen. Scan the lot code on your bottle to see its full certificate.
panel: Heavy metals: lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury

howToRead.a: Thymoquinone is a small aromatic molecule, a quinone, that gives Nigella sativa seed oil much of its peppery character. Laboratories report it as a percentage of the oil by weight, measured by gas chromatography or liquid chromatography against a reference standard.

The seed’s chemistry depends on the cultivar, the soil, the season, how long the seed was stored, and how warm the press ran. Two honest lots from the same farm can differ. That is why we publish a number per lot rather than printing one number for all time.

Peroxide value, in milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram, counts the primary oxidation products in an oil. It is a freshness measure: a low value means the oil has not begun to go rancid. It rises with heat, light, air, and age, which is why the bottle is amber and the storage line says cool and dark.

Gas chromatography separates the oil into its fatty acids, mostly linoleic and oleic in Nigella sativa, and reports each as a percentage. It is a fingerprint of the seed and a check that nothing else was blended in.

The laboratory reports lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury against its detection limits, and screens for total plate count, yeast and mold, and specified organisms. We show the laboratory’s wording and figures as issued.

name: Blackseed Oil
tagline: The original. One seed, one ingredient, one certificate per lot.
short: Single-ingredient Nigella sativa seed oil, cold pressed and bottled in amber glass. Every lot ships with a published laboratory certificate.
long: Most blackseed oil is sold on folklore. Ours is sold on a certificate. Each lot is pressed cold from one harvest, bottled unrefined and unblended, and released only after an independent laboratory has reported thymoquinone, fatty-acid profile, freshness, heavy metals, and a microbial screen. The number on your bottle’s lot page is that laboratory’s, not ours.
intendedUse: A daily spoonful of seed oil, taken straight or stirred into food.
sensory: Bold, peppery, a little bitter. Deep amber-gold. A big herbal aroma. This is an unrefined seed oil, not a neutral one.

howTo.title: Straight up
howTo.body: One dropper, with or after a meal. Let it sit on the tongue a moment before swallowing.

howTo.title: In food
howTo.body: Stir into honey, yogurt, or a smoothie, or drizzle over salad, labneh, or warm bread. Never heat it.

directions: Shake gently. The oil is unfiltered and may show natural sediment.
Take one dropper, about 1 mL, with or after a meal.
Never heat it. Stir into food after cooking, not during.
storage: Cool, dark place. Refrigerate after opening.

faq.q: Why publish a certificate for every lot?
faq.a: Because thymoquinone and freshness vary with the harvest and the press. A single number printed once on a label would be a marketing decision. A certificate per lot is a laboratory result, and it is the only number we will show you.
Yes. Honest blackseed oil is peppery, slightly bitter, and aromatic. A bland oil has usually been refined, diluted, or stored too long.

faq.q: Which size should I start with?
faq.a: The 125 mL bottle is about four months at one dropper a day. The 250 and 500 mL sizes are priced lower per millilitre for households and practitioners.

name: Blackseed Oil Softgels
tagline: The same oil, measured.
short: Our lot-tested oil, 500 mg per softgel, for people who want the measure without the taste.
long: The softgel exists for one reason: not everyone wants to taste blackseed oil every morning. Each softgel carries 500 mg of the same lot-tested, cold-pressed oil that goes into the dropper bottle, sealed in a halal shell that protects it from light and air until you take it.

faq.a: Yes. The gelatin is bovine and halal-certified; certification is attached to each lot record.

faq.q: Two softgels equals how much oil?
faq.a: Two softgels deliver 1,000 mg of oil, roughly one full dropper of the liquid.

name: Golden Hour Saffron Infusion
tagline: Whole saffron threads, steeped for forty days in the oil.
short: Hand-picked saffron infused for forty days in our lot-tested blackseed oil. A spoon in warm milk, over rice, or straight.
long: Saffron and black seed have shared the same kitchen shelf for a thousand years. We steep whole threads, never powder, in cold-pressed blackseed oil for forty days in the dark, then decant. The result is a deep gold oil with the honeyed, hay-and-leather aroma of real saffron and the peppery base of the seed.

faq.a: Saffron’s aroma compounds are oil-soluble but fragile. A slow, cold infusion carries them intact; blending powdered saffron does not.
Yes. We buy ISO 3632 Grade I threads and keep the supplier’s crocin and safranal assay on file with each lot.

name: Culinary Finishing Oil
tagline: Peppery, warm, meant to be tasted.
short: The same cold-pressed oil in a kitchen bottle with a stainless pour spout. Finish lentils, flatbreads, labneh, roasted vegetables, and eggs.
long: Blackseed has been a pantry oil for far longer than it has been a supplement. This is the pressing we are proudest of, in a bottle made to live beside your olive oil. It is not for frying. A thin thread over a finished plate is where it belongs.

faq.a: Think of it as a delicate extra-virgin oil: finish with it, do not fry with it. Heat dulls the aroma.

faq.q: Is it the same oil as the dropper bottle?
faq.a: Yes. Same seed, same press, same lot testing. The difference is the bottle and the spout.

name: Rose & Blackseed Cleansing Oil
tagline: Dissolves the day without stripping it.
short: Grapeseed and blackseed oils infused with damask rose petals, with a touch of plant-derived emulsifier so it rinses clean with water.
long: The first step of an oil-first routine. Light grapeseed carries rose-infused blackseed oil across the skin, lifting sunscreen, makeup, and the day’s film; a sugar-derived emulsifier turns it milky on contact with water so nothing is left behind but soft skin and a faint rose.

faq.a: Grapeseed and blackseed are both light, low-comedogenic oils and the formula rinses off completely. Patch test if you are unsure.
Yes, including waterproof. Hold a soaked fingertip on closed lashes for a few seconds first.

name: Saffron Radiance Face Oil
tagline: The saffron oil. Six drops, morning and night.
short: saffron infused in cold-pressed rosehip, grapeseed and blackseed oils. A fast-absorbing daily face oil with the color of late afternoon.
long: Saffron has been the centrepiece of South Asian skincare for centuries; we wanted it in an oil that actually absorbs. Rosehip and grapeseed give a dry, fast finish, blackseed brings its warm base, and whole Pampore threads steep in the blend for forty days. The color is the saffron’s own.

faq.a: No. The oil is golden in the bottle but sheer on the skin and absorbs fully.

faq.q: Can I use it with retinoids or acids?
faq.a: Yes. Apply it after water-based products have absorbed. If you are using prescription products, ask the clinician who prescribed them.

name: Grapevine Renewal Serum
tagline: From the part of the vine the winemaker prunes away.
short: Grapevine-shoot extract, the plant’s richest source of resveratrol and viniferins, in a light grapeseed and blackseed oil serum for evening use.
long: Vine shoots are cut and burned every winter. We buy them from a single estate, extract them, and carry the extract in cold-pressed grapeseed and blackseed oils. The result is a thin, fast evening serum with a green, slightly tannic scent and nothing in it a winemaker would not recognise.

faq.a: Stilbenes are the family of plant compounds that includes resveratrol and viniferins. Grapevine shoots contain far more than the grape itself, which is why we use the shoot.
Habit, mostly: the serum pairs well with the heavier face oil at night and leaves the morning routine shorter.

name: Blackseed Balm
tagline: A dense, slow-melting salve for dry places.
short: Blackseed oil folded into beeswax, shea, and jojoba with a trace of frankincense. For hands, elbows, heels, cuticles, lips, and the last step of a face routine.
long: The balm is our oil in its most patient form. Beeswax and shea slow it down so it stays where you put it; jojoba carries it in; a trace of frankincense gives it a quiet, resinous lift. There is no water, so there is no need for preservatives.

faq.a: The balm is amber-tinted but absorbs within a few minutes. Let it sink in before dressing.

faq.q: Is it safe for the face?
faq.a: Yes, as a cosmetic moisturizer and final seal. Patch test first and avoid the eye area.

name: Amla & Blackseed Hair Oil
tagline: The Sunday oiling, made properly.
short: Sun-dried amla infused the classical way in cold-pressed sesame and blackseed oils. Massage into the scalp, leave for an hour or overnight, wash out.
long: Across South Asia the week begins or ends with hair oiling. This is that oil, made without shortcuts: whole dried amla fruit steeped for three weeks in cold-pressed sesame, then blended with our lot-tested blackseed oil. It is a pre-wash oil, not a styling product, and it smells of amla and warm seed, not perfume.

faq.a: We do not make that claim. This is a conditioning oil for scalp and lengths. It leaves hair softer and the scalp more comfortable.
Once or twice a week is the traditional rhythm.

name: Scalp & Beard Serum
tagline: Light enough for the scalp, rich enough for the beard.
short: Our blackseed oil cut with jojoba and grapeseed and finished with rosemary leaf oil. A fast-absorbing leave-in for scalp, beard, and the skin beneath.
long: A grooming oil has two jobs: soften the hair and leave the skin under it comfortable. Jojoba mirrors the skin’s own sebum, grapeseed keeps the texture light, blackseed brings its warm aroma, and rosemary gives the finish its clean herbal lift. It absorbs without a film.

faq.a: We do not make that claim. This is a cosmetic conditioning serum.

faq.q: Can I use it after shaving?
faq.a: Yes, sparingly, as a conditioning oil. Patch test first.

name: Blackseed & Mineral Bath Soak

short: Coarse Dead Sea and Epsom salts dressed in blackseed oil, with whole seeds, cornflower petals, and a trace of frankincense.
long: The hammam tradition pairs mineral water with oil; this is that pairing in a jar. Salts are tumbled in our lot-tested blackseed oil so the bath leaves skin soft rather than tight, and a trace of frankincense scents the steam.

faq.q: Will the oil leave a ring?
faq.a: A faint one, which wipes away with a cloth. Rinse the tub while it is still warm.

faq.q: Can I use it as a scrub?
faq.a: The coarse grade is too sharp for skin as a scrub; let it dissolve in the bath.

name: Saffron & Sesame Body Oil
tagline: The daily anointing.
short: Cold-pressed sesame and blackseed oils infused with saffron and a trace of frankincense. For warm self-massage before the shower.
long: Abhyanga, the Ayurvedic practice of warm-oil self-massage, traditionally uses sesame. We keep the sesame and add our lot-tested blackseed oil, a forty-day saffron infusion, and a trace of frankincense. Warm the bottle in a bowl of hot water, take ten minutes, then shower.

faq.a: Keep a dedicated towel for the practice; sesame oil can mark light fabric over time.

faq.q: Can I use it after the bath soak?
faq.a: Yes. Applying it to damp skin after the soak is the shortest route to soft skin.

name: Oud Noir Attar
tagline: Dark wood, warm seed, no alcohol.
short: Hydro-distilled agarwood oil in a base of jojoba and blackseed oil, with labdanum and a trace of frankincense. Worn on the pulse points, it stays close for a working day.
long: An attar is a perfume without alcohol: pure aromatic oils carried in a fixed oil and worn on the skin. Ours begins with plantation agarwood, deep and dry, warmed by our blackseed oil, rounded with labdanum amber and lifted by frankincense. It opens dark and settles into skin-warm wood.

faq.a: Yes. Plantation-grown Aquilaria malaccensis, hydro-distilled. The supplier’s GC-MS profile is kept with each lot.
Attars are the older form of perfume, worn in cultures where alcohol is avoided. Oil also wears closer and longer.

name: Kesar Rose Attar
tagline: Rose with the saffron left in.
short: rose otto and a forty-day saffron infusion over sandalwood, in jojoba and blackseed oil. Honeyed, spiced, and quiet.
long: Kesar is the Hindi word for saffron. This attar pairs it with the rose it has always been paired with, in the way an Indian attar-maker would: over sandalwood, in oil, without alcohol. It smells of rose, then of saffron’s leather-and-honey, then for hours of warm sandalwood.

faq.a: Yes. Certified plantation Santalum album, not wild-harvested.
All three attars are. Rose and saffron have been worn by men across the Middle East and South Asia for centuries.

name: Vigne Verte Attar

long: The third attar is the green one. Grapevine-leaf absolute smells of a vineyard row in early summer: sap, crushed leaf, a little tannin. Vetiver roots it; bergamot opens it; blackseed keeps it from turning sweet.

faq.a: We use furocoumarin-free (FCF) bergamot oil, so no.
